title: Number of 1 Bits
statement:
Given an unsigned 32-bit integer `n`, return how many of its bits are 1 when it is written in binary. This count is often called the Hamming weight.

Constraints: 0 <= n < 2^32, so n is never negative.

examples.explanation: 11 is 1011 in binary, which has three 1s.
128 is 10000000, a single 1 followed by zeros.
That is 32 ones with a single 0 at position 1.

targetComplexity.time: O(number of set bits), at most 32 steps

hints: How can you look at just the lowest bit of a number, and how can you move on to the next bit?
A loop that inspects every bit position works. How many iterations does it need for a 32-bit value?
Can you avoid visiting positions that hold 0 at all?
Try n and n - 1 in binary for n = 12 and n = 8. What happens to the lowest 1 bit and the bits below it?
Combining n with n - 1 using AND removes exactly the lowest set bit, so count how many times you can do that before n reaches 0.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity of your solution, and how many iterations can it take at worst?
How does n & (n - 1) change n, and why does it clear exactly the lowest set bit?
If this function were called millions of times, how could you speed it up with a lookup table?
How would you check whether a number is a power of two using the same trick?
Python also offers bin(n).count('1') and int.bit_count(). What are the trade-offs of using them in an interview?
idealAnswerPoints: Starts with the simple version: test the lowest bit with & 1 and shift right
Improves to n &= n - 1 so the loop runs once per set bit
Explains why n & (n - 1) removes the lowest set bit
States the cost as O(1) for fixed width, or O(k) for k set bits
Mentions a lookup table or the built-in as alternatives
weakAnswerSigns: Converts to a string and counts '1' characters without being able to discuss the bit-level approach
Shifts left instead of right, so the loop never ends
Cannot say how many iterations the loop needs in the worst case

rubric.correctness: Correct counts for 0, powers of two, all ones (2^32 - 1) and mixed bit patterns.
rubric.efficiency: At most 32 iterations in any approach; one iteration per set bit with n & (n - 1) is the target.
rubric.code_quality: A short, clear loop with an explanatory name or comment for the bit trick.
rubric.communication: Explains what the bit trick does with a small binary example before relying on it.
